title: For Every Decision, Think: “What Would Jesus Do?”
paragraphs: For Every Decision, Think: “What Would Jesus Do?”
There are moments in life where the loudest battle is not happening around you.
It is happening inside you.

A text message you are tempted to send.
A compromise nobody would discover.
A relationship God already warned you about.
A business decision that would make money but wound your conscience.
A secret addiction.
A hidden resentment.
A conversation where your flesh wants revenge more than righteousness.

And in those moments, heaven is not merely asking:
“What feels right?”

It is asking:
“What would Jesus do?”

Not culturally.
Not politically.
Not emotionally.
Biblically.

Because modern Christianity has trained many people to ask:
“What can I get away with and still call myself saved?”

But disciples ask:
“How closely can I walk with Christ?”
That is a completely different heart.
The phrase “What Would Jesus Do?” became popular years ago, but many people turned it into a slogan instead of a lifestyle.
The early believers never treated Jesus as a motivational figure.
They treated Him as Lord.
The Greek word used repeatedly in the New Testament is:
κύριος (Kyrios)

Meaning:
Master.
Owner.
Supreme authority.
Not adviser.
Not life coach.
Lord.
Romans 10:9 says:
“If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord…”
The original Greek does not weaken the statement into emotional belief alone.
It declares allegiance.
Submission.
Surrender.
The tragedy of modern culture is that many people want Jesus as Savior without allowing Him to become King over their decisions.
But Scripture reveals that true transformation happens when Christ invades everyday choices.
Not just Sunday worship.
Not just social media Bible verses.
Every decision.
Every reaction.
Every hidden motive.
Jesus Himself said in John 14:15:
“If you love Me, keep My commandments.”
The Greek word for “keep” is:
τηρήσετε (tērēsēte)

Meaning:
to guard carefully,
to watch over attentively,
to preserve through obedience.
Love for Jesus was never meant to stay emotional.
Real love changes behavior.
This is why the question “What Would Jesus Do?” is spiritually dangerous.
Because if we answer honestly, many of us already know the truth.
Jesus would forgive when we want revenge.
Jesus would stay pure where culture says compromise is normal.
Jesus would tell the truth when lies are profitable.
Jesus would walk away from temptation instead of entertaining it privately.
Jesus would choose obedience over popularity.
Jesus would remain compassionate without celebrating sin.
Jesus would pray before reacting.
Jesus would humble Himself instead of proving Himself.
And perhaps most painfully…
Jesus would trust the Father even when suffering did not make sense.
That is where many believers struggle most.
We like Jesus the miracle worker.
But following Jesus the suffering servant costs something.
Isaiah 53 was written hundreds of years before Christ, yet it describes Him with terrifying precision.
The Hebrew says:
אִישׁ מַכְאֹבוֹת (ish mak’ovot)
“A man of sorrows.”
Not merely acquainted with inconvenience.
Acquainted with grief.
Pain.
Rejection.
Betrayal.
Loneliness.
Many people think being Christlike means always appearing victorious.
But Jesus often looked weak to the world.

Silent before accusers.
Patient under abuse.
Compassionate toward sinners.
Merciful toward enemies.
And yet all of heaven declared Him victorious.
One of the deepest misunderstandings in modern Christianity is the idea that asking “What Would Jesus Do?” means asking what is easiest, nicest, or most socially accepted.
No.
Jesus overturned tables.
Jesus rebuked hypocrisy publicly.
Jesus confronted demons.
Jesus spoke hard truths that caused crowds to leave.
Jesus loved perfectly, but He never watered down truth to protect His popularity.
John 1:14 says Jesus came full of:

χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας
(charitos kai alētheias)
“Grace and truth.”

Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Both together.
Perfectly.
That means when believers ask “What Would Jesus Do?” we must reject two extremes:

truth without love,
and love without truth.
Jesus embodied both flawlessly.
This question becomes even more powerful when applied to hidden decisions nobody else sees.
Because character is revealed most clearly in secret places.
The Hebrew word for integrity is often connected to:
תֹּם (tom)

Meaning:
completeness,
wholeness,
moral innocence.
Biblical integrity means being the same person publicly and privately.

The same worshipper in church.
The same believer online.
The same disciple in secret.
And this is where the Holy Spirit begins confronting hearts.
Because some people reading this know they are standing at a crossroads right now.
A relationship decision.
A moral compromise.
A financial temptation.
A hidden conversation.
A private addiction.
A growing bitterness.
And deep down, you already know what Jesus would do.
The real battle is whether you are willing to obey Him.
Luke 9:23 contains one of the most ignored invitations in Christianity:
“If anyone would come after Me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me.”
The Greek word for “deny” is:
ἀπαρνησάσθω (aparnēsasthō)

Meaning:
to utterly refuse association with self-interest.
That destroys the modern gospel of self-worship.
Following Jesus is not adding Him to your plans.
It is surrendering your plans to Him.
Sometimes asking “What Would Jesus Do?” will cost you relationships.
Sometimes opportunities.
Sometimes comfort.
Sometimes reputation.
But obedience to Christ has never been wasted.
Not once.
The disciples lost careers, homes, safety, and eventually their lives.
Yet history remembers emperors as dust while the Gospel still transforms hearts two thousand years later.
Why?
Because truth outlives culture.
Always.
And perhaps one of the most overlooked realities is this:
Jesus did not merely come to improve behavior.
He came to transform identity.
2 Corinthians 5:17 says:
“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
The Greek phrase:

καινὴ κτίσις
(kainē ktisis)

Means:
an entirely new creation of a different quality.
Not patched-up humanity.
New humanity.
This is why Christianity is not behavior modification.
It is resurrection.
The Holy Spirit begins reshaping desires, thoughts, convictions, speech, priorities, and decisions from the inside out.

Suddenly the question changes from:
“How close can I get to sin?”

To:
“How close can I stay to Jesus?”
That is real discipleship.
And the closer you walk with Christ, the more sensitive your conscience becomes.
Things that once felt normal begin grieving your spirit.
Conversations change.
Entertainment changes.
Relationships change.
Priorities change.
Not because religion controls you.
Because love transformed you.
And perhaps the greatest evidence that someone truly knows Jesus is not perfection…
but conviction.
A heart that still wants Him after failure.
A soul that still runs back to grace after falling.
A conscience that refuses to become comfortable in darkness.
Peter denied Christ publicly.
Yet Jesus restored him.
Why?
Because failure was not Peter’s identity.
Surrender was.
Some of you reading this have failed recently.
Badly.

And shame keeps whispering:
“You ruined everything.”
But the cross already knew every sin you would commit before you were born.
The Aramaic words Jesus cried from the cross:
“Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?”
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
carry unimaginable depth.
The sinless Christ entered abandonment so sinners could enter reconciliation.
That is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement.
Substitution.
Mercy.
Redemption.
And now every decision becomes sacred because every decision either moves us closer to Christ or further into spiritual numbness.
The world trains people to follow feelings.
Jesus teaches believers to follow truth.
Even when feelings scream otherwise.
Especially then.

So before the next conversation…
Before the next compromise…
Before the next relationship…
Before the next angry reaction…
Before the next hidden temptation…
Pause long enough to ask:
“What would Jesus do?”
And then ask the harder question:
“Will I obey even if it costs me something?”
Because eternity has never been shaped by comfortable Christians.
It has always been shaped by surrendered ones.
One day every secret thing will stand before God.

Every hidden motive.
Every private decision.
Every compromise.
Every act of obedience.

And in that moment, popularity will not matter.
Excuses will not matter.
Culture will not matter.
Only Christ.
The frightening reality is that many people want the crown without the cross.
But there is no resurrection life without surrender first.
And maybe that is why your spirit feels convicted reading this.
Not condemned.
Convicted.
Because Jesus is still calling you deeper.
Still pulling you closer.
Still offering mercy.
Still transforming hearts willing to surrender.
Sometimes one act of obedience becomes someone else’s rescue.
One quiet decision for Jesus can change the entire direction of a life.
